title: Polynomial-query submodularity testing
formal: Is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error tester for submodularity of arbitrary real-valued set functions using a number of value queries polynomial in the dimension and reciprocal distance? Precisely, do there exist one tester \(A\) in the model below and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), and every function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\), the algorithm \(A^{f}(n,\varepsilon)\) halts and makes at most \(C((n+1)/\varepsilon)^{k}\) value queries on every execution, accepts with probability one if \(f\) is submodular, and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)\ge\varepsilon\)? The constants and program must work simultaneously for all parameters and functions.
why: Submodularity formalizes diminishing returns and underlies many optimization and valuation models. Its value table has exponentially many entries, while algorithms using a submodular value oracle typically see only a small part of it. Polynomial-query testing would determine whether global consistency with that structural assumption can be checked from comparably limited information, with rejection guaranteed for functions requiring widespread changes.
status_note: Source-open under the explicitly recorded one-sided Hamming-distance interpretation. On 15 September 2026, the foundational journal definitions and bounds, Hatami–Vondrák’s manuscript theorem, Blais–Bommireddi’s ITCS 2017 result and Haris–Palit’s published 9 September 2026 work were checked. The later work still records the ordinary-submodularity gap. The original problem page was recovered from its saved full text when live requests failed. This is a bounded status review, not an independent verification of the cited proofs or a Lean formalization.

progress.text: Seshadhri's Bertinoro problem explicitly asks whether \(\operatorname{poly}(n/\varepsilon)\) queries suffice. The listed matroid-rank and coverage directions are separate special questions, not promises imposed on the general target.

Seshadhri–Vondrák give a one-sided tester with query complexity \((1/\varepsilon)^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\) in the small-distance regime. Their Theorem 1.4 also gives examples with few violated squares; that obstruction to this particular local test is not a superpolynomial lower bound for all testers.

Hatami–Vondrák's author manuscript proves an \(\Omega(n^{2}/\log n)\) query lower bound for constant distance in Theorem 1.2. This is still compatible with a polynomial-query tester of larger degree. No later publication venue is inferred for this manuscript.

Blais–Bommireddi prove dimension-independent query bounds for testing \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[0,1]\) under \(\ell_p\) distance for each fixed finite \(p\ge1\) and fixed positive proximity parameter. Theorem 1.1 uses a different distance metric from this card.

Haris–Palit's published k-submodularity paper records the remaining gap for ordinary submodularity. Its constant-query theorem concerns bounded functions in \(\ell_p\) distance; its Hamming-distance results test separate component properties with subexponential bounds. These results do not supply the polynomial Hamming tester asked for here.

sentences: Submodularity expresses diminishing returns for a real-valued function on all subsets of a finite ground set.
The question asks whether a polynomial number of exact value queries can test this property with one-sided error.
Distance is the fraction of table entries that must change to obtain a submodular function, regardless of change magnitude.
Known general upper and lower bounds leave the polynomial-query question unresolved, and constant-query norm-distance results concern a different task.
A resolution would determine how efficiently an oracle’s global diminishing-returns structure can be checked from limited access.

definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) is its set of all subsets, represented by their \(n\)-bit indicator vectors. The class \(\mathcal S_n\) consists of all functions \(g:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[g(S)+g(T)\ge g(S\cap T)+g(S\cup T)\qquad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\] The distance is normalized Hamming distance on the full domain: \[d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)=\min_{g\in\mathcal S_n}2^{-n}\bigl|\{S\subseteq[n]:f(S)\ne g(S)\}\bigr|.\] This minimum exists because attainable disagreement counts form a nonempty subset of the finite set \(\{0,\ldots,2^n\}\). It measures how many table entries change, regardless of the magnitudes of the changes. There is no promise of monotonicity, nonnegativity, bounded range, integrality or normalization at the empty set. The input supplies \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers; the full value table is accessible only through queries. One value query chooses a subset \(S\) and returns the exact real number \(f(S)\), at cost one. Queries may depend on earlier answers and random bits. To specify computation on these exact values, use a finite program with integer and bit-string work storage, real registers initialized by rational constants, exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values, and exact order/equality comparisons. Division by zero is forbidden. The program can request independent fair random bits and can copy queried real values into registers. There is no real-valued advice, noncomputable primitive or other oracle. Only value queries are charged; intervening computation and storage have no quantitative bound, but every execution must terminate after finitely many steps. Acceptance probabilities are over the independent random bits, for each fixed input function. Behavior is unrestricted when \(0<d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)<\varepsilon\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of a tester with every guarantee in the formal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must cover arbitrary real-valued functions and all dimensions and proximity parameters with one finite program and fixed polynomial constants. A negative answer must exclude every such program and every fixed choice of polynomial constants, not only a particular local tester. A result for average value error, a restricted value range, a monotonicity promise, or a constant-dimensional grid does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: A set function assigns a value to each possible subset of a ground set. Submodularity says that adding an element cannot become more valuable merely because the receiving set has grown. Equivalently, it satisfies the union/intersection inequality in the definitions. With \(n\) elements there are \(2^{n}\) values, so inspecting a polynomial number of them is a small fraction of the complete object.

Testing allows an unresolved band of nearby nonsubmodular inputs. The tester must accept genuinely submodular functions and reject functions that disagree with every submodular function on at least an \(\varepsilon\)-fraction of subsets. It is not required to reconstruct the closest submodular function or to decide exact membership for every oracle.

Hamming distance treats any changed entry as one disagreement. In contrast, an \(\ell_p\) distance for finite \(p\) averages the magnitudes of changes. Many tiny discrepancies can therefore contribute little to that norm while affecting a large fraction of the table. The published constant-query result for bounded functions in an \(\ell_p\) metric does not imply polynomial-query testing in the Hamming metric used here.

The saved problem asks both for optimal query complexity and, specifically, whether polynomially many queries suffice. This card selects that explicitly posed polynomial threshold as its single yes/no target. The one-sided-error convention is taken from Definition 1.2 of the cited foundational paper. The finite-program exact-real convention makes the value-oracle interpretation explicit; it is not a claim about bit complexity or noisy measurements.

The existing upper and lower bounds leave a substantial gap: known general testing uses a subexponential number of queries for fixed distance, while a nearly quadratic lower bound rules out much smaller sample budgets. Neither result decides whether some fixed polynomial suffices. Bounds on the frequency of a particular kind of local violation also have a narrower scope than a lower bound against every adaptive tester.
